clinicalPearls: A developmental disorder of the posteromedial proximal tibial physis producing progressive tibia vara (bow legs), distinct from benign physiological bowing
Classified as infantile (onset before about age three), juvenile and adolescent forms, with the infantile type often bilateral
Strongly associated with early walking, obesity and, for the adolescent form, high body mass
The hallmark radiographic finding is depression and beaking of the medial proximal tibial metaphysis with a sharp varus angulation
The metaphyseal-diaphyseal (Drennan) angle helps distinguish pathological Blount disease from self-resolving physiological bowing
Unlike physiological bowing, Blount disease is progressive and does not spontaneously correct, so early recognition matters
Management principles range from bracing in early infantile disease to orthopaedic correction/osteotomy or guided growth for established deformity
reference.pathophysiology: Blount disease reflects abnormal endochondral ossification and growth suppression at the posteromedial aspect of the proximal tibial growth plate. Excessive mechanical compressive load across the medial physis, favoured by obesity and early weight-bearing, is thought to inhibit growth there while the lateral physis continues, producing progressive varus angulation. The persistent malalignment further increases medial compressive force, creating a self-perpetuating cycle (the Hueter-Volkmann principle) that leads to the characteristic depressed, beaked medial metaphysis.
additionalDifferentials: Skeletal dysplasia with bowing (e.g. metaphyseal chondrodysplasia)
additionalInvestigations: Standing full-length lower-limb radiographs to measure varus and the metaphyseal-diaphyseal angle
Assessment for limb-length discrepancy and internal tibial torsion
Serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and vitamin D to exclude rickets
MRI in selected cases to evaluate the physis, cartilage and any bony bar
Serial imaging to document progression versus spontaneous resolution
redFlags: Progressive, worsening deformity failing to resolve as expected for physiological bowing
Markedly asymmetric or unilateral bowing suggesting a pathological cause
Biochemical evidence of rickets or metabolic bone disease
Severe deformity with a physeal bar threatening long-term growth
reference.prognosis: Early infantile disease may respond to bracing, but established or later-onset deformity usually requires orthopaedic correction; outcomes are good with timely treatment, though delayed intervention risks residual deformity and early degenerative knee change.
pitfalls: Mistaking progressive Blount disease for benign physiological bowing and delaying treatment
Failing to exclude rickets as a reversible cause of bowing
Not obtaining standing radiographs, underestimating true alignment
Overlooking obesity as a modifiable contributor and recurrence risk after surgery
references: Rockwood and Wilkins' Fractures in Children
management: Knee-ankle-foot orthosis (bracing) for early infantile disease identified while still mild
Proximal tibial (with or without fibular) osteotomy to realign established or progressive deformity and restore the mechanical axis
Guided growth by lateral tension-band plating or hemiepiphysiodesis in suitable growing children, with physeal bar resection where a bony bar has formed
Weight management and lifestyle intervention for the associated obesity
Serial standing full-length lower-limb radiographs (metaphyseal-diaphyseal angle) to distinguish progression from physiological bowing, time surgery and exclude rickets
Address any associated limb-length discrepancy and internal tibial torsion
Ongoing paediatric orthopaedic follow-up given the progressive, non-resolving nature of the deformity
